title: New York musicians' condescension toward Southern blues singers
summary: Albertson relays Snowden, Wooding and Scott dismissing blues singers; Procope rejects this, saying Southern singers had a culture and accompanists were part of it, like Louis Armstrong.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Bessie, Mamie, Ma Rainey: the classic blues queens

blocks.x: But I remember Elmer Snowden telling me about, you know, the blues singers and people who came up from the south. Musically he didn't think very much of them, you know. Sam Wooding said the same thing. He thought Bessie Smith, for instance, and all those blues singers, they were so slow, he said Bessie would start a verse and he'd go to the bathroom and when he came back she was just finishing the same verse, you know, she was so slow. And Howard Scott said the

same thing, that he didn't really -- it bored him to accompany blues singers because it was all very monotonous, very much the same and very simplistic music. And I've always sensed that maybe there was a little bit of snobbery there by New York musicians, thinking that the people from the south were a little bit primitive.
I understand exactly what you mean, but I never had that --

Yeah, well, those are words, sophistication and whatever. But I always appreciated those people from the south, because they had a culture, and when they said, "My baby left me. My baby left me a mule to ride," or whatever, that was their culture. They were singing their hearts out, telling you, "Please understand me. I'm trying to make you understand." And I don't understand Snowden and Howard Scott talking about they couldn't understand that. That's a lot of crap! Believe me. I don't believe it!

And trumpet players, and clarinet players and musicians accompanying Bessie Smith or Ma Rainey or whoever, they were just a part of what was happening. I don't see how they could say they resented them. Well, of course they were doing their thing.
Maybe they were a little jealous, too.
Louis, he was from the south.
That's right. That's right. And that was Louis' thing.

All through his career. When he left New Orleans and went to Chicago, he was backing up blues singers. And all those records he made when he came to New York with Clarence Williams. He was backing up -- I've got an album home, Louis Armstrong and Bessie Smith. So I can't understand how these people could say that. There wasn't any resentment on my part, believe me.
